title: Relics, honestly
hookLine: Catholics honor the remains of saints as signs of holy lives, not magic

cards: A grandmother's wedding ring, kept in a drawer. A father's reading glasses, still on the shelf years later. A child's first shoe.
Nobody thinks the ring has powers. Nobody prays to the glasses. But nobody throws them away either, because they were close to someone who mattered, and touching them brings that person near.
Hold that drawer in mind. It's the honest way into a word that makes some people uneasy.

teach.b: A relic is something that remains from a saint: a piece of the body, often a fragment of bone, or something the saint used or wore.
Catholics keep relics in churches, in altars, in small glass cases called reliquaries, and honor them. Honor is the key word.
In Catholic teaching, relics are venerated, not worshipped. Worship belongs to God alone.
A relic is honored because of the person it points to, and because of what Catholics believe about the body: that it was a temple of the Holy Spirit and will rise again.
The Psalms put the feeling simply, in the Douay-Rheims: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." The Bible has stories behind the practice too.
In the books of Kings, a dead man is lowered into the grave of the prophet Elisha, touches his bones, and comes back to life.

In the Acts of the Apostles, cloths that had touched Paul are carried to the sick, and they recover. Catholics read those as God acting through holy people, even through what they leave behind. Now the honest part.
Relics have been faked, stolen, sold and fought over.

teach.h: NOT A CHARM; NEVER FOR SALE.
teach.b: The Church's own teaching warns against superstition, against treating any object as if it worked by itself, like a charm, and Church law forbids selling relics at all.

teach.h: PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.
teach.b: So a relic, rightly understood, is not a lucky object. It's closer to that drawer at home: a body, or a thing, that once belonged to someone who loved God, kept close so the memory stays warm.

how: Catholic churches often keep relics of saints in altars or reliquaries; on feast days relics may be exposed for veneration, and people may kneel, pray nearby or touch the reliquary, while Church law forbids selling relics.

games.q: a stranger at a market offers you a small bone, 'from a saint,' at a good price. what does Church law say?
o: buy it and give it to a church.
buy it if it comes with a certificate.
games.why: Church law forbids selling relics at all. the practice is about honoring a holy life, not trading in objects.

practice: Some churches keep a relic in or under the altar, or in a side chapel, where people stop for a minute.
For now, think of an object you've kept because of someone you loved, its weight, its color, where it lives in your home, and let the person come to mind through it.
If you pray, pray for them, or ask a saint to pray with you; if not, hold the object and the person together, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Relic. Something that remains from a saint, their body or something they used, honored for the holy life it points to, never worshipped.

orig.note: Latin: remains, what is left behind; the word Catholics use for the relics of saints.

carryVoice: Your line: bodies that loved god. Honored, never worshipped. Day nine hundred fifty, done.
